origin_region: Uva Province · Badulla, Bandarawela and Haputale (900–1,600 m)
cultivar: Assam-type seedling bushes and TRI clones
processing: Fully oxidised orthodox black tea in broken grades; during the dry season a dry wind from the west stresses the leaf and concentrates its aromatic compounds, giving the famous pungent 'Uva character'.
harvest_season: Year-round, but the July–September dry season is the quality window; outside it the teas are plainer.
appearance_dry: Small, tightly twisted dark broken leaf, slightly reddish.
appearance_liquor: Deep orange-red, bright, with a coppery rim.
taste_profile: Pungent and distinctive: a cooling, wintergreen-like aroma over a strong, brisk body with firm tannin and a sweet finish.

brewing.notes: Stands up to a full boil and takes milk well.

vintage_note: Sold through the weekly Colombo auction by estate and grade; the July–September 'Uva season' invoices from estates such as Uva Highlands, Dyraaba, Aislaby and Demodera command the highest prices of the year and are what the big blenders chase for breakfast blends. Buy a current-season lot and drink within a year; tea labelled simply 'Uva' from outside the season will be milder.
description:
Uva is the eastern slope of Sri Lanka's central highlands, around Badulla, Bandarawela and Haputale at roughly 900 to 1,600 metres, and it makes the most distinctive of the Ceylon teas. For a few months each year a dry wind pours over the hills from the west, stressing the bushes and concentrating the aromatic compounds in the leaf; the teas made in that window have a pungent, almost wintergreen-like character that blenders prize and that nothing else in Sri Lanka reproduces.

Manufacture is orthodox, mostly broken grades (BOP, BOPF), with a wither, rolling, quick oxidation and firing. Outside the dry season the same estates make pleasant but ordinary tea; the 'Uva season' from roughly July to September is the whole point.

The cup is deep orange-red and bright, strong and brisk with a cooling, mentholated aroma, firm tannin and a sweet finish. It stands up to a full boil and takes milk well, and it is the backbone of many classic English breakfast blends. Three to four minutes with water off the boil, with or without milk.

It is sold through the weekly Colombo auction by estate and grade, and the July-to-September invoices from estates such as Uva Highlands, Dyraaba, Aislaby and Demodera fetch the highest prices of the year; the big blenders fight over them. Buy a current-season lot and drink it within a year. Tea labelled simply 'Uva' outside the season will be milder.

Thomas Lipton's original Ceylon estates were in these hills, around Haputale, which is why Uva tea turns up in so many old advertisements.
sources_note: The trade name for the seasonal dry wind ('Cachan') was left out as unverified; estate names from memory.
